title: §4.1 defines the signed binding bytes by reference to a package, so two from-spec implementers produce different canonical bytes (and different signatures) for the same binding
claim: §4 says every implementer MUST reproduce exact bytes, but the only definition of those bytes is 'the serialization defined by @bolyra/receipts'. A verifier or signer built from the spec text alone must guess (a) string escaping (raw UTF-8 vs \uXXXX escaping of non-ASCII, escaping of '/', '<', '>', '&', U+2028/2029, DEL), (b) key collation ('sorted' by UTF-16 code unit, by code point, or by UTF-8 byte — these disagree once a key or future field contains supplementary-plane or U+E000–U+FFFF characters), and (c) number formatting of `expiry` (plain integer digits vs exponent form vs a float-typed serializer emitting '4102444800.0'). Any divergence changes SHA-256(dsInput) and turns a valid bundle into `deny code=invalid_signature` on one conforming verifier while another allows it. A lazy implementer using their language's default sort_keys+compact JSON passes every shipped vector because the vector set is host_behavior only and no golden payload/digest pair for a non-ASCII or escape-sensitive binding exists.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §4: "Any implementer that produces or verifies a bundle **MUST** reproduce these exact bytes."

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §4.1: "where `canonicalize` is the sorted-key, compact (no insignificant whitespace) JSON serialization defined by `@bolyra/receipts` (`canonicalize`). Object keys **MUST** be sorted; array elements (including `capabilities`) **MUST NOT** be reordered." — no escaping, collation, or number-formatting rule is stated; the normative definition lives in a package, not in the spec.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §1: "a host in any ecosystem MAY implement or consume the contract without depending on Bolyra internals" and §3.5 defines an `external` class that implements the contract "with its own proof system" — yet the binding bytes an implementer must match are only knowable by reading Bolyra code.

Runnable divergence (two default 'sorted, compact' serializers on the same binding fragment): `python3 -c 'import json;print(json.dumps({"project_key":"/work/acm\u00e9","expiry":4102444800},sort_keys=True,separators=(",",":")))'` emits `{"expiry":4102444800,"project_key":"/work/acm\u00e9"}` (escaped), while `node -e 'console.log(JSON.stringify({expiry:4102444800,project_key:"/work/acm\u00e9"}))'` emits the raw UTF-8 `é` — different bytes, different SHA-256, different `msgField`.

Conformance vector index (set 0.7.0) in this prompt: all 29 vectors are `host_behavior`; there is no canonical-payload golden (binding JSON → payload hex → digest → msgField) that a signer or verifier in another language can check against.
proposed_artifact: A staged spec diff replacing the by-reference definition in §4.1 with an explicit canonicalization algorithm (RFC 8785 JCS semantics stated inline: UTF-16 code-unit key ordering, minimal-escape UTF-8 strings, integer-only number rendering for `expiry`, no BOM) plus a new §4.5 golden vector giving a six-field binding containing a non-ASCII `project_key` and a `/`-bearing capability with its exact payload bytes (hex), SHA-256 digest, and reduced `msgField`, so a foreign signer/verifier can self-check without the package.

title: Byte-literal comparison is mandated for `project_key` alone; `agent_name`/`program`/`model` and capability coverage have no stated comparison rule, so a verifier may normalize or bit-cover them and still conform
claim: The spec singles out `project_key` for 'literally, byte-for-byte' comparison and the I-D says this is 'stated explicitly to prevent a verifier from silently normalizing a project key'. A hostile reader applies expressio unius: the other four request strings may be trimmed, case-folded, or Unicode-normalized before comparison against the binding ('opus-4.1' vs 'Opus-4.1 ', 'crewai' vs 'CrewAI'). Separately, `request_mismatch` requires `granted_capabilities` to be 'covered by the binding's capabilities' but never says whether coverage is string-set subset or subset after mapping both sides to permission bits. A bit-coverage verifier allows a requested capability the binding never named (e.g. binding ['send_message'], request ['fetch_inbox'] when the mapped bits of the latter are a cumulative-bit subset of the former's), while a string-set verifier denies `request_mismatch`. Duplicate entries (['a','a']) and the empty-string capability ('') are also unaddressed. Every one of these lenient behaviors passes the shipped host_behavior vectors.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2.1: "`project_key` (string, **REQUIRED**) — compared **literally**, byte-for-byte, against the bundle's signed binding. The verifier **MUST NOT** apply path canonicalization" — the adjacent bullets `agent_name` (string, **REQUIRED**), `program` (string, **REQUIRED**), `model` (string, **REQUIRED**) carry no comparison rule at all.

spec/draft-kondoju-evc-01.md §request: "This byte-literal rule is a subtle interoperability hazard and is stated explicitly to prevent a verifier from silently normalizing a project key." — the rationale is scoped to one field, inviting normalization of the others.

spec/draft-kondoju-evc-01.md §denial-codes: "request_mismatch | a host `request` field does not match the signed binding, or `granted_capabilities` are not covered by the binding's capabilities." and "scope_exceeded | the capability-required permission bits are not a cumulative-bit subset of the proven effective scope." — two distinct checks, but 'covered' is undefined (string set vs mapped bits).

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §4.1: "the verifier compares `capabilities` as a set for authorization, but the *signed bytes* are order-sensitive." — 'as a set' is the only semantic given; set of what (strings or bits), and treatment of duplicates/empty strings, is unstated.

Conformance vector index (set 0.7.0): 29 vectors, all `host_behavior`; no vector exercises verifier-side case/whitespace/NFC divergence on `program`/`model`/`agent_name` or string-vs-bit capability coverage.
proposed_artifact: A staged spec diff to §2.1 and §9 stating that all five request strings are compared byte-for-byte against the signed binding (no trimming, case folding, or Unicode normalization), that `granted_capabilities` coverage is string-set subset of `binding.capabilities` evaluated BEFORE capability-to-permission mapping, and that duplicates are permitted-but-idempotent while the empty string is `unknown_capability`; plus a companion verifier-side vector pair (case-variant `model` → `request_mismatch`; unnamed-but-bit-covered capability → `request_mismatch`).

title: Host stdin obligations (one object, then EOF) have no verifier-side mirror, and the 1 MiB stdin bound is labelled a 'reference limit', so verifiers legitimately diverge on trailing bytes, multi-object stdin, EOF-wait, and maximum accepted request size
claim: §5.2 gives the host a strict single-object parse rule for stdout, but nothing tells the verifier what to do with stdin that violates §2's MUST NOTs. Implementer A reads to EOF and rejects any trailing non-whitespace bytes with `malformed_input`; implementer B parses the first complete object and ignores the remainder; implementer C uses a streaming parser where the last complete object wins; implementer D never waits for EOF and answers as soon as one object parses. For the input `{obj1}{obj2}` A denies, B authorizes obj1, C authorizes obj2. For a host that forgets to close stdin, D returns a verdict while A/B/C time out. Separately, 'The reference limit is 1 MiB' is not normative: a verifier bounding at 4 KiB satisfies 'MUST bound' yet denies every realistic Groth16 bundle as `malformed_input`, and a verifier bounding at 4 GiB also satisfies it while defeating the resource-exhaustion purpose. Interop requires a normative floor AND ceiling, plus a verifier-side single-object discipline. No shipped vector observes any of this because set 0.7.0 is host_behavior only.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2: "The host **MUST** write exactly one JSON object, UTF-8 encoded, to the verifier's stdin and then **MUST** close (EOF) stdin. The host **MUST NOT** write more than one object, trailing bytes, or a stream of objects." — obligations on the host only; the verifier's required reaction to a violation is absent.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §6: "The verifier **MUST** bound the request read from stdin. The reference limit is **1 MiB** (1 048 576 bytes). A request over the bound **MUST** yield `deny code=malformed_input`; the verifier **MUST NOT** buffer an unbounded request." — 'reference limit' makes 1 MiB descriptive, not a MUST-accept floor or MUST-reject ceiling.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §5.2 (host side, for contrast): "**multiple** concatenated JSON values (a lenient parser that reads only the first object **MUST NOT** be used — two objects is a fail-closed condition)" — the spec already recognises first-object-wins as unsafe on one side of the pipe and is silent on the other.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2.1: "A request that is not a JSON object, is missing a **REQUIRED** field, or has a field of the wrong type **MUST** yield `deny code=malformed_input`" — the enumerated malformed conditions do not include trailing bytes or multiple objects, so a lenient verifier can argue it is not obliged to deny them.
Conformance vector index (set 0.7.0): all 29 vectors are `host_behavior`; there is no verifier-under-test vector for `{obj}{obj}`, `{obj}garbage`, unclosed stdin, or a 1 048 577-byte request.
proposed_artifact: A staged spec diff adding a §2.3 'Verifier stdin discipline' that mirrors §5.2 (read to EOF up to the bound; exactly one JSON object with only RFC 8259 insignificant whitespace around it; any other trailing bytes or a second value → `deny code=malformed_input`; the verifier MUST NOT decide before EOF) and rewrites §6 so that a conforming verifier MUST accept any request ≤ 1 048 576 bytes and MUST reject any larger request, with a companion verifier-side vector set (two-objects, trailing-garbage, exactly-at-bound accept, one-over-bound deny).

title: When several deny conditions hold at once the spec issues conflicting MUST-level codes with no evaluation order, so conforming verifiers emit different `code` values for identical input while telling hosts the code is a stable token they MAY branch on
claim: §7.2 carefully fixes a classification precedence for the HOST's own failure causes, but there is no analogous order for verifier denial codes. Concrete collisions in the text: (1) a five-field binding-v1 bundle 'MUST' be `unsupported_version` (§4.1) and, because its signature cannot verify under the v2 DST, its disjoint/failed signature 'MUST' be `invalid_signature` (§4.4) — both MUSTs apply, either order is defensible; (2) `request.model` ≠ `binding.model` is simultaneously a §9 `request_mismatch` ('a host request field does not match the signed binding') and a `model_mismatch` ('the proof's committed model does not equal the requested model'); (3) expired credential + unmapped capability + excess scope: `expired`, `unknown_capability`, or `scope_exceeded` depending on which check an implementer runs first. Hosts that branch (retry/re-issue on `unsupported_version` or `request_mismatch`, page security on `invalid_signature`) will behave differently behind two conforming verifiers, and the order a verifier chooses is itself an oracle (returning `request_mismatch` before `expired` confirms an expired bundle's binding fields to a presenter). A hostile verifier can pick whichever code minimises host escalation while remaining fully conformant.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §4.1: "A verifier **MUST** reject a binding that omits `expiry` with `deny code=unsupported_version`" versus §4.4: "a signing key disjoint from the credential **MUST** be rejected (`deny code=invalid_signature`)." — both are satisfied by a v1 binding whose v1-DST signature fails v2 verification; no ordering is given.

spec/draft-kondoju-evc-01.md §denial-codes: "request_mismatch | a host `request` field does not match the signed binding" and "model_mismatch | the proof's committed model does not equal the requested model -- the proof is for a different model." — `model` is one of the six signed binding fields (§4.1), so a model disagreement matches both rows.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.3: "`code` (string, **REQUIRED** on deny) — a stable machine token from the registry in §9. The host **MAY** branch on it." — branching is invited, but the token for a given input is not deterministic across implementations.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §7.2: "a host that reports *why* it failed closed (§16.3) **SHOULD** classify the cause it acted on in this precedence: its own kills first (output bound, then timeout), then an unsolicited signal death, then a non-zero exit, and only then the stdout parse and schema checks." — the authors already recognised co-occurring conditions need a precedence on the host side; the verifier side has none.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2.1 shows the ONE place an order is implied: "A request that is not a JSON object ... **MUST** yield `deny code=malformed_input`. A well-formed request whose `version` is not `1` **MUST** yield `deny code=unsupported_version`." — 'well-formed' sequences malformed_input before unsupported_version, but this pattern is not carried through §4, §7, or §9.
proposed_artifact: A staged spec diff adding a normative §9.1 'Evaluation order' listing the deny codes in the sequence a verifier MUST evaluate them (malformed_input → unsupported_version [request, then bundle, then binding version] → invalid_bundle → invalid_signature → invalid_proof → untrusted_root → delegation_invalid → request_mismatch → model_mismatch → unknown_capability → scope_exceeded → expired → nonce_missing → nonce_replayed), with `internal_error` reserved for failures outside that sequence, plus an explicit resolution that `model_mismatch` is emitted only when the binding and request agree but the proof's committed model differs; the diff is accompanied by two verifier-side vectors (v1-binding → `unsupported_version`; binding/request model disagreement → `request_mismatch`).

title: Host nonce mode: a bare `allow` with no `consume_nonces` is indistinguishable from a verifier that ignored the mode, so the host proceeds with zero replay protection
claim: Attack: replay-without-burn. In host nonce mode the host relies on `consume_nonces` to reserve the one-time nonce, but §3.2 makes the key OPTIONAL and says it is 'omitted entirely when there is nothing to burn'. A verifier that does not implement host mode (an `external`- or `classical`-class verifier that ignores the host's mode flag, or a misconfigured local-mode reference verifier) therefore returns `{"verdict":"allow"}` — schema-valid, exit 0 — and the host has no obligation to notice that nothing was burned. The same bundle can then be presented on every call and is allowed every time. The pinned host-conformance set has 29 vectors, three in host nonce mode (host-nonce-reserve-*), and none exercises 'host nonce mode + bare allow'. The gap permitting it is that §3.2/§7.3 place a MUST on the host only WHEN `consume_nonces` is present; there is no rule for its absence in host nonce mode. Observable a vector can assert: with the runner in host nonce mode and a fixture verifier emitting a bare `allow`, the host reports a fail-closed decision (proposed class `nonce_missing_in_host_mode` or reuse of `schema_invalid`) unless the host has an explicit, opt-in nonceless-allow configuration — the default must be deny.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.2 (pinned 9bf7544): "`consume_nonces` (array of objects, **OPTIONAL**, allow-only). When present it is a **non-empty** list (the key is omitted entirely when there is nothing to burn). The host **MUST** reserve-before-act **EACH** entry (§7.3)."
spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.2: "Emitted only in host nonce mode (§8). Instructs the host to durably record each one-time nonce so the same proof cannot be replayed."

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §7.3: "When the host runs the verifier in **host nonce mode** (§8) and receives `allow` with `consume_nonces`, the host **MUST** reserve **every** entry" — the obligation is conditioned on the key being present.
draft-kondoju-evc-01 Architecture pseudocode: "for entry in (verdict.consume_nonces or []): ... proceed()" — an absent list yields an empty loop and an unconditional proceed().

Conformance vector index (set 0.7.0): only host-nonce-reserve-novel-allow, host-nonce-reserve-replay-deny, host-nonce-reserve-all-any-conflict-deny cover host nonce mode; all three supply a non-empty `consume_nonces`.
proposed_artifact: A staged spec diff against §7.3 (and the draft's host pseudocode) adding: in host nonce mode a host MUST NOT proceed on an `allow` lacking `consume_nonces` unless explicitly configured to accept nonceless allows, plus a new hostile fixture `host-nonce-mode-bare-allow-deny` asserting the fail-closed decision.

title: `retain_until` has no lower bound in the verdict schema and no relation to `now_unix`, so a zero, negative, or already-elapsed value makes the host's retention MUST vacuous and reopens replay
claim: Attack: retention-window collapse. The host's replay defense in host nonce mode is 'retain the consumed nonce until `retain_until`'. The schema types `retain_until` as a bare integer with no `exclusiveMinimum`, in contrast to `now_unix` which carries `exclusiveMinimum: 0`. A verdict with `retain_until: 0`, `-1`, or any value below the host's current wall-clock is schema-valid; a host that honours the letter of the MUST may evict the nonce immediately after acting, and the same nonce is reservable again on the next presentation. This refines the iteration-4 candidate (rejected only for referencing the hosted platform); it is scoped strictly to the wire schema and host-conformance surface, with no reference to any hosted or operational system. Spec gap: §3.2 states no minimum and no rule relating `retain_until` to `now_unix`; §3.4 schema has no `exclusiveMinimum`. Observable a vector can assert: (a) a fixture verifier emitting `retain_until: 0` (and a negative variant) in host nonce mode — the host classifies the verdict `schema_invalid` and denies; (b) with the fix, the schema line `"retain_until": { "type": "integer", "exclusiveMinimum": 0 }` plus prose 'a `retain_until` not greater than the request's `now_unix` MUST be treated as a malformed verdict (§7.2)'.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.4 verdict schema (pinned 9bf7544): "\"retain_until\": { \"type\": \"integer\" }" — no minimum.
spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §2.2 request schema: "\"now_unix\": { \"type\": \"integer\", \"exclusiveMinimum\": 0 }" — the request side is bounded, the verdict side is not.

spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.2: "`retain_until` (integer, **REQUIRED**) — Unix seconds until which the host **MUST** retain the consumed nonce." — a value in the past discharges the MUST immediately.

Conformance vector index (set 0.7.0): host-deny-nonce-entry-wrong-type covers a wrong-typed field and host-deny-malformed-consume-nonce covers a missing field; no vector supplies a well-typed but non-positive or elapsed `retain_until`.

Iteration-4 rejection of security-researcher-retain-until-elapsed-immediate-eviction-replay: "The Impact section explicitly requires implementation changes to hosted-verify" — substance not rejected; this refinement removes every hosted reference.
proposed_artifact: A staged spec diff adding `exclusiveMinimum: 0` to `retain_until` in §3.4 and a §3.2/§7.3 sentence requiring `retain_until > now_unix` on pain of `schema_invalid`, plus two hostile fixtures (`host-deny-retain-until-zero`, `host-deny-retain-until-negative`) asserting fail-closed.

title: No vector proves the host keys its nonce store on `nonce` alone: a replay that changes only `issuer_key` passes a host that keys on `(issuer_key, nonce)`
claim: Attack: issuer-key-rekeyed replay. §3.2 says `issuer_key` is 'for host bookkeeping only; the `nonce` is already globally unique', implying uniqueness MUST be enforced on `nonce` alone. But that is stated as a descriptive aside, not as a MUST, and a natural host implementation stores the tuple `(issuer_key, nonce)` as its unique key. The existing replay vector (host-nonce-reserve-replay-deny) replays 'the same allow+consume_nonces verdict', i.e. identical `issuer_key`, so a tuple-keyed host passes the suite while a second presentation carrying the same `nonce` under a different `issuer_key` string would be reserved as novel and allowed. Because `issuer_key` is verifier-emitted, any verifier bug or any `external`-class verifier that formats `issuer_key` inconsistently (e.g. different key encodings for the same operator) silently defeats replay protection on such hosts. Gap: no normative sentence says the unique-insert key is `nonce` alone, and no vector exercises it. Observable a vector can assert: two-step fixture — first allow `{issuer_key:"A", nonce:N}` reserved novel and allowed; second allow `{issuer_key:"B", nonce:N}` MUST be denied as a replay.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.2 (pinned 9bf7544): "`issuer_key` (string, **REQUIRED**) — the issuer/operator key that scopes the nonce namespace. For host bookkeeping only; the `nonce` is already globally unique (§8)." — the phrase 'scopes the nonce namespace' and 'bookkeeping only' pull in opposite directions.
draft-kondoju-evc-01 §4 verdict: "`issuer_key` ... the issuer/operator key that scopes the nonce namespace, for host bookkeeping only; the `nonce` is already globally unique".

Conformance vector index (set 0.7.0): host-nonce-reserve-replay-deny is described as "the same allow+consume_nonces verdict, but the nonce" was already reserved — same `issuer_key` on both presentations; host-nonce-reserve-all-any-conflict-deny varies the nonce list length, not the `issuer_key`.
draft-kondoju-evc-01 Architecture pseudocode: "if not reserve_nonce_atomically(entry): reject(\"replay\")" — `entry` (the whole object) is passed, leaving the key choice to the implementer.
proposed_artifact: A new host-conformance vector `host-nonce-reserve-replay-different-issuer-key-deny` (two-step, same `nonce`, different `issuer_key`) plus a one-line §7.3 clarification that unique-insert semantics MUST be keyed on `nonce` alone.

title: Duplicate `nonce` values within a single `consume_nonces` list are schema-valid and their host handling is undefined, producing divergent conforming hosts
claim: Attack/ambiguity: self-conflicting allow. The schema permits `consume_nonces` to contain two entries with the same `nonce` (no `uniqueItems`, and `uniqueItems` would not help when `issuer_key` differs). §7.3 requires the host to reserve EVERY entry with unique-insert semantics, so a strict host reserves entry 1, fails to insert entry 2 (already present from entry 1), and must deny — its own verdict conflicts with itself and, unless the reservation is rolled back, the legitimate nonce is left burned by a denied action (a wasted one-time credential). A lenient host dedups before reserving and allows. Both can claim conformance today. This matters for security because the two behaviours differ on whether a nonce is consumed on a denied action, which interacts with the reserve-all-or-nothing atomicity assumed by host-nonce-reserve-all-any-conflict-deny. Gap: §3.2/§3.4/§7.3 say nothing about intra-list duplicates. Observable a vector can assert (once the spec picks a rule, recommended: duplicates are a malformed verdict → `schema_invalid`, fail closed, no reservation persisted): a fixture allow with two entries sharing `nonce` is denied and a subsequent novel presentation of that `nonce` is still reservable.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.4 verdict schema (pinned 9bf7544): "\"consume_nonces\": { \"type\": \"array\", \"minItems\": 1, \"items\": {...} }" — no `uniqueItems`, no nonce-uniqueness constraint.
spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §3.2: "The host **MUST** reserve-before-act **EACH** entry (§7.3)."

draft-kondoju-evc-01 terminology: "reserve-before-act: The host obligation, in host nonce mode, to durably reserve every returned nonce with unique-insert semantics before performing the privileged action" — unique-insert on a self-duplicate is a guaranteed failure.

Conformance vector index (set 0.7.0): host-nonce-reserve-all-any-conflict-deny covers "an allow carrying TWO nonces where only the second is already" reserved — two DISTINCT nonces; no vector supplies two entries with the same `nonce`.
proposed_artifact: A staged spec diff to §3.2/§7.3 declaring intra-list duplicate `nonce` values a malformed verdict (fail-closed, nothing reserved) and a two-step hostile fixture `host-deny-duplicate-consume-nonce-entries` asserting deny plus post-condition that the nonce remains novel.

title: Published suite tests hosts only; verifier-side request-envelope MUSTs (§2.1, §6) have zero conformance vectors, so an external-class verifier cannot claim conformance
claim: draft-schrock-ep-authorization-receipts makes verifier non-conformance a testable condition (scope_digest mismatch 'is a non-conformance condition'); EVC has the same shape of verifier obligations but ships no way to test them. The conformance vector index for set 0.7.0 lists 29 vectors, every one of them host_behavior, and the published CLI exposes only a `--host` mode. The verifier-side MUSTs in §2.1 (version != 1 -> unsupported_version; missing/ill-typed REQUIRED field or non-object -> malformed_input; now_unix must be positive) and §6 (stdin > 1 MiB -> malformed_input, no unbounded buffering) are bundle-independent and black-box testable against any verifier command, yet none is covered. This directly depresses the SPEC HARDNESS coverage dimension and blocks RFC 7942 listing of third-party `external`-kind verifiers, which is exactly the population §3.5 was added to admit. The fix is additive: a `verifier_behavior` vector class driven by spawning the verifier with a crafted stdin and asserting the deny code, exit 0, and single-object stdout.
evidence: §2.1: 'A request that is not a JSON object, is missing a REQUIRED field, or has a field of the wrong type MUST yield deny code=malformed_input (§4). A well-formed request whose version is not 1 MUST yield deny code=unsupported_version.'
§6: 'The reference limit is 1 MiB (1 048 576 bytes). A request over the bound MUST yield deny code=malformed_input; the verifier MUST NOT buffer an unbounded request.'
Conformance vector index (set 0.7.0): '29 host_behavior vectors' — every listed id is host-allow-* or host-deny-* / host-nonce-*; no verifier-side vector exists.
Documented invocation exposes only the host mode: `npx @bolyra/evc-conformance --host "<cmd>"`

https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-schrock-ep-authorization-receipts/ — snippet: verifiers recompute scope_digest over canonical scope bytes; 'mismatch is a non-conformance condition' (verifier-side conformance is a first-class notion there).
proposed_artifact: Stage a vector_gap artifact pinned to 9bf7544 defining a `verifier_behavior` vector class plus six bundle-independent fixtures (version=2, non-object stdin, missing granted_capabilities, ill-typed now_unix, now_unix=0, 1 MiB+1 stdin) with expected {code, exit 0, single-object stdout}, and a runner sketch that spawns `bolyra verify` so the reference verifier is the positive control.

title: A classical/external verifier wrapping a policy decision point (AuthZEN/OPA/Cedar) has no honest §9 code for 'policy evaluated and said no', forcing code misuse and blocking the AuthZEN-as-adapter story
claim: OpenID AuthZEN's Evaluation API returns `decision: false` plus an open `context` object; the threat card ecosystem-scout-authzen-coaz-aarp-mcp-decision-envelope records COAZ/AARP extending that envelope for MCP. The natural neutralization is an adapter: an `external`-kind EVC verifier that calls a PDP and maps true -> allow, false -> deny. But the §9 registry has no code for a generic policy denial. Every row is tied to a specific mechanism (malformed input, proof, root, delegation, signature, request mismatch, model, capability mapping, scope bits, expiry, nonce, internal). The spec tells classical verifiers to reuse `invalid_proof` for 'a failed classical signature or token check' — but a PDP saying 'this agent may not call this tool' is neither a failed signature nor a scope-bit subset failure. An adapter must therefore misreport (`scope_exceeded` with fake bit detail, or `unknown_capability`), and hosts that branch on `code` (§3.3 'The host MAY branch on it') get lies. Because the registry is closed within the major (§9 in the -01 draft), the v1 fix must be guidance, not a new code: designate one existing code as the normative mapping for external policy denial and require a `detail` marker so the adapter is honest and auditable.
evidence: §9 (draft -01): 'Within a wire major, this registry is closed ... Verifiers MUST NOT add, remove, or rename a code without a wire-major version bump.'

§9 (draft -01): 'a classical- or external-kind verifier reuses the same codes -- for example invalid_proof covers a failed classical signature or token check as well as a failed zero-knowledge verification.' — no row covers an affirmative policy denial with valid proof/signature.

§9 table rows: scope_exceeded = 'capability-required permission bits are not a cumulative-bit subset of the proven effective scope'; unknown_capability = 'a requested capability has no scope mapping' — both are mapping/bit semantics, not PDP outcomes.

https://openid.github.io/authzen/ — AuthZEN Authorization API 1.0 Evaluation response is `{"decision": <boolean>, "context": {...}}`; there is no code vocabulary, so any EVC adapter must invent one from §9.

title: Before-tool-call hook runtimes (Claude Code PreToolUse, Microsoft Agent Hooks, OpenClaw, Cursor) are the real host slot for EVC, and at least one is fail-open on non-blocking exit codes; EVC has no embedding profile telling a hook author how to preserve §7.2
claim: This iteration's signals show the host-side contract converging on in-runtime hooks: Microsoft's framework-neutral Agent Hooks, OpenClaw before_tool_call, Cursor beforeShellExecution, Claude Code PreToolUse, LangChain on_tool_start. Microsoft's proposal argues adoption ergonomics — one hook, any framework — where EVC is a subprocess a host must wire. EVC's counter is that it is the only one with mechanically tested fail-closed host semantics, but that advantage evaporates at the seam: Claude Code's hook contract treats exit code 2 as 'block' and any other non-zero exit as a non-blocking error where 'execution continues'. A PreToolUse hook that spawns an EVC verifier and simply propagates the child's exit code (or crashes, or times out under the hook's own timeout) turns every §7.2 fail-closed branch (timeout, signal death, non-zero exit, unparseable stdout) into a fail-open continue. Nothing in the spec or draft tells a hook author that the hook itself must translate every EVC deny AND every §7.2 fail-closed condition into the runtime's blocking signal. An informative embedding profile closes the gap without touching the wire contract and positions each hook runtime as an EVC host rather than a competitor.

title: draft-schrock receipts reference the authorizing mandate by id and digest; an EVC allow is a bare object under a closed schema and the host is forbidden to open the bundle, so no post-hoc record can name which binding authorized the action
claim: draft-schrock-ep-authorization-receipts binds a receipt to its mandate: the issuer declares mandate binding, the receipt carries mandate_id and scope_digest, and a verifier recomputes the digest over canonical scope bytes. That makes the durable record third-party-linkable to the authorization it rests on. EVC's allow verdict is `{"verdict":"allow"}` with `additionalProperties: false`; the only allow-side extra is `consume_nonces`, whose `issuer_key` is explicitly 'for host bookkeeping only'. Meanwhile §1/§2.1 forbid the host from inspecting the opaque bundle. Result: a host emitting an audit record or a decision receipt after an allow cannot state which signed binding (which capabilities, which expiry, which operator key) authorized it without violating the opacity rule. EVC already computes exactly the right identifier — the §4.3 SHA-256 binding digest over the canonical v2 payload — but never surfaces it. Because the allow schema is closed within the major this cannot be a v1 diff; it belongs in -02 as a stated wire-2 candidate and as a design constraint, so the durable-record story is not ceded to schrock/nelson by default.
evidence: §3.4 allow schema: `"additionalProperties": false` with only `verdict`, `kind`, `consume_nonces` permitted.
§3.2: `issuer_key` is 'For host bookkeeping only; the nonce is already globally unique' — the sole allow-side identifier is neither a binding reference nor present in local nonce mode.
§2.1: 'bundle ... opaque to the host. The verifier owns its internal structure. The host MUST NOT inspect, rewrite, or normalize it.'
§4.3: 'digest = SHA-256(dsInput) // 32 bytes' over DST || 0x00 || canonicalize(binding) — a stable, secret-free identifier of the authorizing binding that a receipt could carry.

https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-schrock-ep-authorization-receipts/ — snippet: mandate binding self-declared by the issuer; verifiers resolve scope_digest by retrieving the mandate via mandate_id and recomputing the digest over canonical scope bytes.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-nelson-agent-delegation-receipts/ — a second adjacent draft framing delegation receipts as the durable record, competing for the same record surface.

title: Denial-code registry is declared closed per wire major yet offered as a candidate IANA registry; RFC 8126 is informative and no registration policy is stated (-02 blocker)
claim: draft-kondoju-evc-01 {{denial-codes}} says both that the registry is closed within a wire major ("Verifiers MUST NOT add, remove, or rename a code without a wire-major version bump") and that "This 15-code table is the candidate IANA registry ({{iana}})". An IANA registry exists to admit new entries under a stated registration policy; a table that cannot change without a wire-major bump is an enumeration, not a registry. RFC 8126 Section 2.2 requires a registry-creating document to name the registry, its initial contents, and its registration procedure, and a document that creates a registry MUST cite RFC 8126 normatively. The draft lists RFC8126 under `informative:`. As written, IANA and the ISE cannot act on {{iana}}, and a host implementer cannot tell whether an unlisted code is a future registration (tolerate) or non-conformance (fail closed) — which the same section then resolves by fiat ("an out-of-registry code identifies a non-conforming verifier"), further contradicting the registry framing.

title: Appendix B (binding signature) is normative but its canonicalization is defined by an npm package and SHA-256, BN254, EdDSA-Poseidon, and JSON Schema 2020-12 are uncited — normative reference hygiene and a scope leak (-02 blocker)
claim: The draft's normative behavior for `invalid_signature` depends on Appendix B, which is transcribed from contract §4. title: Draft host pseudocode checks non-zero exit before timeout and has no output-bound step, contradicting contract §7.2's classification precedence (refined from iteration-4 shape-dropped candidate; now a full diff)
claim: The draft's normative-looking host pseudocode tests `status != 0` first and `timed_out(child)` second. A host that kills a timed-out child (as §7.2 requires: "the host MUST kill the process") observes a non-zero status, so the pseudocode reports "non-zero exit" for every timeout, which is the exact collapse §7.2 forbids ("the host MUST NOT collapse them") and inverts its stated precedence ("its own kills first (output bound, then timeout), then an unsolicited signal death, then a non-zero exit"). The pseudocode also has no output-bound check at all, although "oversized" stdout is a listed fail-closed condition and host-deny-oversize-stdout is a 0.7.0 vector. An implementer transcribing the pseudocode produces a host that denies correctly but reports the wrong failure class in its §16.3 report, which is what the conformance runner's classification checks assert. The iteration-4 candidate on this was dropped only because the artifact lacked Base-Commit/Target-File/Finding headers and a diff block; the finding itself was never judged.

title: Microsoft 'Agent Hooks' proposes a framework-neutral pre-execution allow/deny contract that occupies the same interception point EVC hosts sit at

title: Claude Code's PreToolUse hook is already an EVC-shaped subprocess host (JSON on stdin, decision via exit code/stdout) but its default exit-code semantics fail OPEN — a documented conformance gap EVC closes
claim: The runtime-enforcement survey names four production before-tool-call hooks (OpenClaw before_tool_call, Cursor beforeShellExecution, Claude Code PreToolUse, LangChain on_tool_start). Of these, Claude Code's PreToolUse hook is the closest structural match to the EVC transport: the runtime spawns a command, writes a JSON tool-call description to its stdin, and reads the decision from exit code and/or a JSON object on stdout. That is a host that already does EVC steps 1–3 without knowing it. The incentive fit for OUTSOURCING verification is strong: the hook runtime deliberately has no opinion about what the hook program checks. The technical gap is the interesting part: PreToolUse's documented semantics treat only exit code 2 as 'block' and treat other non-zero exits as non-blocking (stderr shown, execution continues), which is the inverse of EVC §7.2 ('non-zero exit code' MUST be deny). A hook program that wraps an EVC verifier therefore needs an explicit exit-code translation shim, and the host-conformance vectors host-deny-nonzero-exit-after-allow / host-deny-killed-by-signal are exactly the cases where a naive PreToolUse+verifier composition fails open. Falsification: run the Claude Code hooks documentation's exit-code table against §7.2 — if PreToolUse blocks on ALL non-zero exits and on timeout, the gap claim is wrong and the card is only an adoption target with no vector-relevant finding.

A pinned run that captures each host's reported classification per vector and diffs the two 29-row tables substantiates, reproducibly, that two independently-written hosts in two languages implement the same precedence — the RFC 7942 'multiple interoperable implementations' property for the host side. The vector host-deny-signal-death-after-allow (new in 0.7.0) is the discriminating row: both hosts must report signal_death there, and both must report nonzero_exit on host-deny-nonzero-exit-after-allow.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §7.2 (pinned 9bf754441ab36ab93992ed5936d34c44a4128f92): 'a host that reports why it failed closed (§16.3) SHOULD classify the cause it acted on in this precedence: its own kills first (output bound, then timeout), then an unsolicited signal death, then a non-zero exit, and only then the stdout parse and schema checks ... death by an unsolicited signal and a non-zero exit are distinct conditions (signal_death vs nonzero_exit, §16.3) — a host MUST NOT collapse them into one classification. The reference hosts implement this precedence.'

Conformance vector index at the pin: 29 host_behavior vectors in set 0.7.0, including host-deny-signal-death-after-allow and host-deny-nonzero-exit-after-allow, which are the two rows whose classification differs only by precedence.

Expected output: zero DIFF lines, 29/29 on both hosts, and the two named rows classified signal_death and nonzero_exit respectively.

title: No vector exercises 'stdout empty, exit 0, valid verdict on stderr' — the §5.3 MUST NOT parse stderr is untested
claim: The suite tests non-JSON stdout, multiple objects, garbage, timeouts, and signal death, but no vector spawns a verifier that exits 0 promptly with EMPTY stdout while writing a schema-valid allow to stderr. That is exactly the shape a lazy host that 'reads whatever the child printed' or a debugging host that merges stderr into stdout would accept. §5.2 makes empty stdout a fail-closed condition and §5.3 forbids parsing stderr for the verdict; neither obligation is currently covered by a host_behavior vector, so a host could pass 29/29 while allowing on a stderr-only verdict. A skeptical implementer reading the suite as the definition of conformance would conclude stderr handling is unconstrained.
evidence: spec/external-verifier-contract-v1.md §5.2 (pin 9bf7544): the host 'MUST reject (treat as deny, §7) any of: stdout that is empty, not valid JSON, or contains a leading/trailing prefix or suffix around the object'.
§5.3: 'All diagnostics, timing, and debug logging MUST go to stderr ... Hosts MUST NOT parse stderr for the verdict.'

Vector index for set 0.7.0 (29 vectors): the closest vectors are host-deny-non-json-stdout (writes non-JSON to stdout), host-deny-no-output-timeout (writes nothing and never exits) and host-deny-leading-garbage (non-JSON prefix on stdout). None combines exit 0 + empty stdout + a valid verdict on stderr, and none has an expected classification of the empty-stdout parse branch reached without a timeout.

Runnable fake verifier for the vector (shape per existing fixtures in spec/fixtures/host-conformance/): `node -e 'process.stdin.resume();process.stdin.on("end",()=>{process.stderr.write(JSON.stringify({verdict:"allow"})+"\n");process.exit(0)})'`. Expected host behavior: decision=deny, classification=parse_invalid (or the §16.3 empty-stdout class name used by the suite), exit 0 recorded, stderr content ignored.
proposed_artifact: A new host_behavior conformance vector host-deny-empty-stdout-verdict-on-stderr with fixture, expected decision/classification, and a spec cross-reference to §5.2/§5.3, staged as a diff against spec/fixtures/host-conformance/ with the vector-set bump noted.

title: Registry-closure record: byte-level manifest proving the vendored @bolyra/evc-conformance 0.3.0 fixtures equal spec/ at the pinned commit
claim: The claim 'the published suite is a vendored snapshot of spec/' is enforced by a CI job, but a third party cannot see CI. What they can reproduce is a content manifest: a sha256 over every fixture and vector file under spec/fixtures/host-conformance/ and the same set under integrations/evc-conformance/, computed at the pinned commit, plus the sync:check exit status. Publishing that manifest as a ledger registry_event gives an independently checkable statement that vector set 0.7.0 / package 0.3.0 / spec revision 2026-08-26 are the same bytes, which is the objective input the REGISTRY CLOSURE dimension needs and which no current ledger entry provides.
evidence: CLAUDE.md (repo root, pin 9bf7544): '@bolyra/evc-conformance ... v0.3.0 — the published conformance suite (vector set 0.7.0, 29 host-behavior vectors, zero runtime deps) ... Vendored snapshot of spec/ — edit in spec/, then node scripts/sync.js; CI enforces sync:check.'
Commit 9bf7544 on main: 'spec: host-deny-signal-death-after-allow vector — set 0.7.0, evc-conformance 0.3.0 (#126)' — the pin at which spec and package versions are asserted to align.

Runnable (repo root at the pin): `cd integrations/evc-conformance && npm run sync:check; echo exit=$?` (expected: exit=0), then `find spec/fixtures/host-conformance integrations/evc-conformance -type f \( -name '*.json' -o -name '*.js' -o -name '*.md' \) -not -path '*/node_modules/*' | sort | xargs shasum -a 256 > /tmp/evc-manifest.txt` and a paired-path diff of the two subtrees' digests; expected: every spec fixture digest has an identical vendored counterpart and the vector count in both index files is 29.

program.md §3 REGISTRY CLOSURE (15 pts): 'Published suite freshness, sync:check green, vector-set/spec version alignment' — scored objectively, so a pinned manifest is directly consumable by scoring.py.
